sentences.text: When I was young, it was easy to hurt me.
My father told me what he thought I should do.
I have thought about his words ever since.
He said, "Think before saying bad things about people.
Not everyone has had the good things you have had."
He said no more.
We could tell each other much with few words.
I knew he meant much more than that.
So I often wait before I judge anyone.
This can help me learn about many strange people.
Some talk a long time without saying anything interesting.
An abnormal mind can quickly see this in someone normal.
Such people want to share things with that person.
People at college called me a politician.
That was not fair.
I knew the secret pain of wild, unknown men.
I did not ask for most of their secret talk.
I would act as if I had gone to sleep.
Sometimes I would act busy, or make fun of them.
I did this when I knew secret talk was coming.
Young men often use words they have taken from others.
You can also see that they leave things out.
To wait before we judge takes hope without an end.
I am still afraid I might miss something.
I must remember what my father said.
Some people are born with more good in them.
He said this as if we were better than others.
I say it in that way too.
I have been boasting about my tolerance.
But there are things I cannot put up with.
The way people act may rest on hard rock.
Or it may rest on wet marshes.
After a point, I do not care which it is.
Last fall, I came back from the East.
I wanted the world in uniform.
It should stand at moral attention forever.
I wanted no more riotous excursions.
They gave me privileged glimpses into the human heart.
Only Gatsby did not make me feel that way.
This book has his name.
Gatsby was everything I really looked down on.
What if personality is an unbroken series of successful gestures?
Then there was something gorgeous about him.
He had great sensitivity to the promises of life.
He was like machines that register earthquakes 10,000 miles away.
This was not that flabby impressionability.
I mean that things change you too much.
People make that sound important: “creative temperament.”
His was an extraordinary gift for hope.
He had a romantic readiness for what life might bring.
I have never found this in anyone else.
I probably never will.
No, Gatsby turned out all right in the end.
But something preyed on Gatsby.
Foul dust floated in the wake of his dreams.
That made me lose interest in the sorrows of men.
Their sorrows came to nothing.
Their happy times did not last.
I lost interest in those happy times too.
This was only for a while.
My family has been well-to-do and important here.
This is a city in the Middle West.
This has been true for three generations.
The Carraways are a close family.
We say our family comes from the Dukes of Buccleuch.
But my grandfather’s brother really started our family line.
He came here in '51.
He sent another man to the Civil War.
That man went in his place.
He started a business.
He would sell things used to make and fix things.
He would sell them to other business people.
My father is still in charge of that business.
I never saw this great-uncle.
People say I look like him.
The painting hangs in the office of my father.
He looks like a hard man in that painting.
I finished school at New Haven in 1915.
My father finished there 25 years before me.
A little later, I took part in the Great War.
I call it a late “Teutonic migration.”
I mean a war, as if people were just moving.
I did enjoy fighting back so much.
I came home restless because of that.
I once felt the Middle West was a warm centre.
It felt like the centre of the world.
Now it felt like the ragged edge of the universe.
So I decided to go East.
I would learn the bond business.
Everyone I knew worked in that business.
I thought it could pay one more single man.
All my aunts and uncles talked about my plan.
They talked as if choosing a prep school for me.
At last, they said, "Well, yes."
They looked very serious and not quite sure.
My father agreed to give me money for a year.
After some delays, I came East in spring, 1922.
I thought I would stay there for good.
To find rooms in the city made the most sense.
But the days were warm.
I had just left wide lawns and friendly trees.
A young man at work had an idea.
We could share a house in a town.
We would go into the city for work each day.
That sounded like a great idea.
He found a weather-beaten bungalow.
It was like a house made of cardboard.
It was 80 a month.
At the last moment, work sent him to Washington.
So I went to the house in the country alone.
I had a dog for a few days.
Then he ran away.
I also had an old Dodge and a Finnish woman.
She made my bed and cooked breakfast.
She muttered Finnish wisdom to herself.
She did this over the electric stove.
For a day or so, I felt alone.
Then one morning a man stopped me on the road.
He had come here after I did.
"How do I get to West Egg village?"
He asked helplessly.
I told him the way.
As I kept walking, I no longer felt alone.
I could show people the way.
I felt like a pathfinder and an original settler.
Without trying, he made me feel at home here.
The sun was out.
New leaves were growing on the trees in great bursts.
They were growing like things in a fast film.
I felt sure life was starting again with summer.
I had felt that way before.
For one thing, there was so much to read.
The young, breath-giving air could give me so much health.
I bought 12 volumes about banking, credit, and investment securities.
They stood on my shelf in red and gold.
They looked like new money from the mint.
They were promising to show the shining secrets of money.
Only Midas, Morgan, and Maecenas knew those secrets.
I had a great plan: read many other books too.
I was interested in what people read and write.
This was when I was in college.
One year, I wrote editorials for the Yale News.
They were very serious and said things everyone already knew.
Now I would bring all that back into my life.
Again, I would become a “well-rounded man.”
Such a man is the most limited of all specialists.
That is more than just a smart saying.
After all, life is better seen through a single window.
By chance, I rented a house in a strange place.
Few communities in North America were as strange.
It was on a slender island.
The island goes straight east from New York.
It had two strange formations of land.
These were only two of its strange natural things.
They are 20 miles from the city.
They look like two very big eggs.
Their contour is the same.
Only a bay is between them.
They go out into Long Island Sound.
That is salt water in the Western hemisphere.
They are not perfect ovals.
Their contact end is crushed flat.
They are like the egg in the Columbus story.
Gulls that fly overhead must always wonder at their resemblance.
People on the ground find something else more interesting.
Their shape and size are the same.
They are different in every other way.
I made my home at West Egg.
It was, well, the less fashionable of the two.
But that simple name does not tell the whole truth.
They were different in a strange, rather sinister way.
My house was at the very end of the egg.
It was only 150 feet from the Sound.
It was squeezed between one very big house and another.
Each house was 12,000 or 15,000 for one season.
The house on my right was very big.
It was an imitation of a Hôtel de Ville.
That government building was in Normandy.
There was a tower on one side.
It was very new under a thin beard of ivy.
There was a marble swimming pool.
It had over 40 acres of lawn and garden.
That was the great house of Gatsby.
Or rather, I did not actually know Mr. Gatsby.
A gentleman of that name made his home there.
My own house was an eyesore, but a small one.
People had overlooked it.
I could see the water.
I could see part of my neighbour’s lawn too.
Being near millionaires made me feel better.
All this was 80 dollars a month.
Across the bay was fashionable East Egg.
Its white palaces glittered along the water.
My story of that summer really started one evening.
I drove to East Egg for dinner with the Buchanans.
Daisy was my second cousin once removed.
I had known Tom at college.
Just after the war, I spent two days with them.
That was in Chicago.
Her husband had been great at many physical things.
He played football at New Haven.
He was one of their most powerful ends ever.
People across the country knew of him.
At 21, he was already great at that one thing.
Everything afterward felt less wonderful.
His family was very rich.
Even at college, people thought he spent too much.
Now he had left Chicago and come East.
The way he came East took your breath away.
He even brought polo ponies from Lake Forest.
Someone from my own generation had that much money.
It was hard to believe.
I do not know why they came East.
They spent a year in France for no special reason.
Then they kept moving, never at rest in one place.
They went where rich people played polo together.
Daisy said on the phone they would stay for good.
I did not believe her.
I could not know what she really felt.
But I thought Tom would always keep moving.
He would keep looking a little wistfully.
He would want the dramatic turbulence of some football game.
He could never get that game back.
I drove over to East Egg one warm, windy evening.
I went to see two old friends.
Really, I knew almost nothing about them.
Their house was even more elaborate than I expected.
It was a cheerful red-and-white Georgian Colonial mansion.
It looked out over the bay.
The lawn ran from the beach towards the front door.
It ran for 0.25 miles.
It was like something jumping over sundials and brick walks.
It was like jumping over burning gardens.
At the house, it was drifting up the side.
It went up in bright vines.
It was as if its run kept it going.
There was a line of French windows at the front.
They were glowing with reflected gold.
They were wide open to the warm, windy afternoon.
Tom Buchanan was standing on the front porch.
He was in riding clothes, with his legs apart.
He had changed since his years at New Haven.
Now he was a strong man of 30.
His hair was light and close to gold.
His mouth looked rather hard.
He was supercilious, as if better than other people.
His eyes were full of light.
They made him look too proud of himself.
They took over his face.
They made him look as if always leaning aggressively forward.
His riding clothes had an effeminate look, meant for show.
Even these clothes could not hide his enormous power.
He seemed too big for his glistening boots.
He strained their top lacing.
A lot of muscle moved when his shoulder moved.
You could see it under his thin coat.
His body could move things with great force.
It was a cruel body.
His voice was a gruff, husky tenor.
It made him seem even more ready for a fight.
He talked like a father who knows better than you.
There was a little contempt in his voice.
He talked this way even to people he liked.
Some men at New Haven had great hate for him.
This was what he seemed to say:
"I am stronger and more of a man than you.
That does not make my opinion about these things final."
We were in the same club at school.
That was in our last year.
We were never very close.
I had always felt he did think well of me.
I thought he wanted me to like him.
That wish was hard and defiant, with some wistfulness.
We talked on the porch for a few minutes.
We were in the sun.
"I have a nice place here," he said.
His eyes kept moving quickly all around, without rest.
He turned me around by one arm.
His broad, flat hand moved across what we could see.
There was a sunken Italian garden.
There was half an acre of deep, pungent roses.
A snub-nosed motorboat bumped the tide offshore.
"It belonged to Demaine, the oil man."
He turned me around again, politely and abruptly.
"We will go inside."
We walked through a high hallway into a bright room.
The room was rosy-coloured.
There were French windows at either end.
They made it seem only just part of the house.
The windows were open a little.
They were gleaming white against the fresh grass outside.
The grass seemed to grow a little way inside.
A breeze went through the room.
It blew curtains in one end and out the other.
They moved like pale flags, twisting up toward the ceiling.
The ceiling looked like a frosted wedding-cake.
Then the breeze moved over the wine-coloured rug.
Its shadow moved like wind on the sea.
Only the enormous couch was completely still.
Two young women were buoyed up on it.
It was like an anchored balloon.
Both women were in white dresses.
The dresses kept moving in the air.
It was as if they had made a short flight.
The flight had taken them around the house.
Now the air had blown them back inside.
I must have been standing there for a little while.
I could hear the hard, quick sound of each cover.
A picture on the wall also made a deep sound.
There was a big, deep sound.
Tom Buchanan had shut the window at the back.
The air stopped moving through the room.
Each window cover came down, little by little.
So did each cover on the floor.
The women no longer looked as if in the air.
One woman was born later than the other.
I did not know her.
She was at her end of the divan.
Her body was at full length.
She did not move at all.
Her chin was up a little.
She looked as if balancing something likely to fall.
She may have seen me from the side.
But she gave no sign of it.
I almost said sorry in a quiet voice.
I felt like I should not have come in.
The other girl was Daisy.
She tried to get up and moved forward a little.
Her face said she wanted to do the right thing.
Then she gave a strange but lovely little laugh.
I started laughing too and went forward into the room.
"I am so happy that I cannot move."
She gave another laugh.
It was as if she had said something very smart.
She took my hand for a moment.
She looked up at my face.
Her look made a promise.
There was no one she wanted to see more.
She often made people feel this way.
In a quiet voice, she told me the last name.
The girl with her head back was called Baker.
Some people say she wants them to move close.
They say she does it by using a quiet voice.
I had heard them say this about Daisy.
It did not matter.
Her voice was still lovely.
Miss Baker's lips moved a little.
She nodded at me so little I almost missed it.
Then she quickly tipped her head back again.
It was as if her object had tottered a little.
That had given her a little fright.
Again, I almost said sorry.
People who need no help almost always make me wonder.
I feel surprise and respect.
I looked back at Daisy.
She started to ask me questions.
Her voice was quiet and full of feeling.
I wanted to hear her voice go up and down.
Each time she talked, it was like new music.
You would never hear this music again.
Her face was lovely and sad.
Her eyes were full of light.
Her mouth was full of life and feeling.
But the way her voice made people feel was special.
Men who had loved her found it difficult to forget.
Her voice made them want to listen.
It was like music, with a quiet call to listen.
She made you think she had just done wonderful things.
It was a promise of more wonderful things next hour.
I told her about my day in Chicago.
I had stopped there on my way East.
12 people sent their love through me.
"Do they miss me?"
She called out in a very happy voice.
"The whole town is very sad."
"Every car has its left rear wheel painted black.
It is like a mourning wreath.
A crying sound goes all night along the north shore."
"How lovely this is!"
"Let us go back, Tom."
"Let us go tomorrow."
Then she changed what we were talking about.
"You should see the baby."
"I would like to see her."
"She has gone to sleep."
"She is three years old."
"Have you never seen her?"
"I have never seen her."
"You should see her."
She started to say more about the little girl.
Tom Buchanan had been moving around the room without rest.
He stopped and put his hand on my shoulder.
"What are you doing, Nick?"
"I am a bond man."
"Who do you work with?"
I told him the name.
"I have never heard of them," he said.
He was quite sure.
This made me a little angry.
"You will hear of them," I said.
My answer was short and not very nice.
"You will if you stay in the East."
"Do not worry," he said.
"I will stay in the East."
He looked at Daisy, then back at me.
He did seem ready to hear something more.
"I would be a damn fool to live anywhere else."
Miss Baker said, "I absolutely agree!"
She talked so quickly that I moved in surprise.
She had said nothing since I came into the room.
She did seem to feel the same surprise.
Her mouth came open as if she wanted sleep.
Then she quickly got to her feet.
Each move was quick and easy.
"My body is hard to move," she said.
"I have been lying on this seat for so long.
I cannot remember when I first came here."
"Do not look at me," Daisy said.
"I tried all afternoon to take you to New York."
Someone brought a drink for each of the four people.
They came from the room where the food was kept.
Miss Baker said, "No, thank you."
"I am working hard to get ready to play.
I am absolutely serious about it."
Tom looked at her.
He did seem not to believe her.
"You really are?"
He finished his drink in a moment.
He made the full drink seem very small.
"How do you ever get anything done?
I cannot understand it."
I looked at Miss Baker.
I tried to think what work she did.
It was a pleasure to look at her.
She was a slender, small-breasted girl.
Her body was straight.
She kept her shoulders back like a young cadet.
Her grey eyes looked tired from the sun.
She looked back with polite curiosity.
I was interested in her, and she in me.
Her face was wan, lovely, and not quite happy.
I now thought I had seen her somewhere before.
Perhaps I had seen a picture of her.
"You live in West Egg," she said.
She made it sound like a bad place.
"I know somebody there."
I started to say that I knew nobody there.
I did not finish.
"You must know Gatsby."
"Do you mean Gatsby?"
Daisy asked this and wanted an answer.
"Which Gatsby do you mean?"
I was about to say that Gatsby was my neighbour.
But someone said dinner was ready before I could answer.
Tom Buchanan put his tense arm hard under mine.
He made me leave the room.
It was like moving a checker to another square.
The two young women went out ahead of us.
Their hands were set lightly on their hips.
They moved slenderly and without hurry.
They went to a rosy-coloured porch, open toward the sunset.
Four candles flickered on the table.
The wind was less strong now.
"Why do we need this light from fire?"
Daisy asked this with an angry look.
She snapped them out with her fingers.
"In two weeks, the day will have the most light.
No other day in the year will have more."
She looked at all of us with a happy face.
"Do you watch for the day with the most light?
I mean the most light in the year.
Do you always watch for it and then miss it?"
"I always watch for that day.
Then I miss it."
"We should plan something," said Miss Baker.
Her mouth came open as if she wanted sleep.
She took her seat at the table.
It was as if she were going to bed.
"All right," said Daisy.
"What shall we plan?"
She turned to me as if she needed help.
"What do people plan?"
Before I could answer, she looked at her little finger.
Her expression was full of wonder.
"Look at this!"
"I hurt it," she said in an angry voice.
We all looked.
Her knuckle was black and blue.
"You did it, Tom," she said.
She made it clear that it was his fault.
"I know you did not mean to hurt me.
But you did hurt me."
"I married a man who can hurt people.
That is why this has happened to me.
He is such a great, big, strong man."
She did not finish what she was saying.
"I hate being called big like that," said Tom.
He was angry.
"I hate it even when you are kidding."
Daisy called him big in the same way again.
Sometimes she and Miss Baker talked at once.
They did not try to make anyone listen.
They were playing with words that meant little.
They did not talk too much.
Their talk was calm, like their white clothes.
Their eyes had no wish for anything.
They did not look at anyone in a personal way.
The women were here with Tom and me.
They did seem to think we were fine company.
They tried a little to be nice.
They tried a little to give or enjoy some pleasure.
They knew dinner would soon be over.
A little later, the evening would be over too.
They would put it behind them without much thought.
This was very different from life in the West.
There, people had to hurry through each evening.
They went quickly from one part to the next.
They always had hope for something that did not happen.
Or they were afraid of the very moment.
"You make me feel uncivilized, Daisy," I said.
I was on my second glass of claret.
It was corky, but still quite impressive.
"Can you talk about food that comes from the ground?
Or something like that?"
I did not mean anything special by this.
But someone said something I did not expect.
"The world we know is coming to an end."
Tom said this with great force.
"I have come to expect terrible things."
"Have you read The Rise of the Coloured Empires?
It is by a man called Goddard."
"No, I have not," I said.
His way of speaking was quite a surprise.
"It is a fine book.
Everybody should read it."
"We white people must be careful.
If not, other people will completely take over."
"It is all work to learn how the world works.
That work makes it clear this is true."
"Tom is getting very deep," Daisy said.
Her sad look did not seem to come from thought.
"He does read a book with very deep thought.
Such a book has long words in it."
"What was that word?"
She started to say more but did not finish.
"This is all about how the world works," said Tom.
He looked at her as if tired of waiting.
"This man has worked out the whole thing."
"We white people are the ones in control.
We must watch out for other people.
If we do not, they will take control."
"We must beat them down," said Daisy.
Her voice was very quiet.
She quickly shut one eye while looking at the sun.
She did it with great force.
The sun was still hot.
"You should live in California," Miss Baker started to say.
But Tom stopped her by moving hard in his seat.
"The idea is that we are Nordics."
"I am, and you are, and you are."
He stopped for just a moment.
Then he moved his head to say Daisy was, too.
She quickly shut one eye at me again.
"We made all the things that make life work.
We worked out how the world works and made art.
We did all of that."
"Do you see what I mean?"
He thought very hard about what he was saying.
It almost made me feel sorry for him.
He was even more happy with himself than before.
But being happy with himself did not seem enough anymore.
Almost at once, the phone started to ring inside.
The man who brought our food left the outside table.
Daisy took this chance to move close to me.
"I will tell you a family secret," she said.
Her voice was quiet but very happy.
"It is about the man who works here.
I mean the part of his face over his mouth.
It is between his eyes."
"Do you want to hear about that part?"
"That is why I came over tonight."
"He was not always a butler.
He once worked for some people in New York.
He was their silver polisher.
They had a silver service for 200 people.
"He had to do this from morning till night.
At last, it hurt that part of his face."
Miss Baker said, "Things went from bad to worse."
"Yes, that is right."
"Things went from bad to worse.
At last, he had to leave his job."
For a moment, the sun gave her face light.
It made her look beautiful and full of life.
As I heard her voice, I had to move forward.
I felt I could not take in enough air.
Then the light left her face, little by little.
I almost felt sorry to see the light go.
It was like children leaving a nice street at night.
The man who brought our food came back.
He talked close to the side of Tom Buchanan's head.
He talked with a very quiet voice.
Tom looked angry and moved his seat back.
He went inside without saying a word.
Daisy moved close to me again.
She did seem more alive now that Tom was gone.
Her voice was happy and full of music.
"I love to see you at my table, Nick."
"You remind me of a rose, an absolute rose.
"Does he not make you think of that?"
She turned to Miss Baker and wanted her to agree.
"Is he not exactly like that lovely thing?"
This was not true.
I am not even a little like a rose.
She was making up her words as she talked.
But I felt her strong wish to be close.
Her quick, wonderful words had strong feeling in them.
They made you feel that you were important to her.
She had something to keep her mouth clean during dinner.
Now she gave it a quick throw to the table.
She said she had to leave and went inside.
Miss Baker and I looked quickly at each other.
We were careful not to show what we thought.
I was about to speak.
She quickly moved up in her seat.
She said, "Be quiet."
Her voice told me that I must be careful.
People talked with great feeling in the next room.
Their talking was quiet.
Miss Baker moved close to hear.
She did not hide that she wanted to hear.
For a moment, I could almost understand the words.
Then the talking got quiet again.
Then it was full of strong feeling again.
We could hear more of its sound.
Then it completely stopped.
"That Mr. Gatsby you talked of lives next to me."
I started to tell her more.
"Do not talk."
"I want to hear what happens."
"Is something happening?"
I asked because I did not know anything was wrong.
"Do you mean you do not know?"
Miss Baker asked this in real surprise.
"I thought everybody knew."
"I do not know."
She started to answer, then stopped for a moment.
"Tom has another woman in New York."
"He has another woman?"
I said those words again.
I had no idea what she meant.
Miss Baker moved her head to say yes.
"She should know better than to call him during dinner.
Do not you think?"
Before I could really understand, I heard clothes moving.
I also heard the sound of big feet.
Tom and Daisy were back at the table.
"Nothing could be done about it!"
Daisy said this, trying hard to sound happy.
Her voice was strong, but she did not feel calm.
She took a seat and looked hard at Miss Baker.
Then she looked at me and kept talking.
"I looked outside for a minute.
It is a lovely night to be in love.
"There is a bird on the lawn.
I think it must be a nightingale.
Perhaps it came over on Cunard or White Star Line.
It will not stop making a song."
Her voice was like a song.
"It makes you feel in love, Tom, does it not?"
"Very romantic," he said.
Then he talked to me in a sad voice.
"I want to take you down to the stables.
We can go after dinner, if it is light enough."
The phone inside made a sound that did surprise us.
Daisy moved her head at Tom to say no.
That stopped the talk about his team, and everything else.
The last five minutes at the table felt broken.
I remember the candles being lit again, for no reason.
I wanted to look straight at everyone.
Yet I also wanted to avoid all their eyes.
I could not guess what Daisy and Tom were thinking.
Miss Baker looked strong and hard to fool.
But even she must have kept thinking about the phone.
The phone was like one more person, making 5.
It kept calling for attention with a strong voice.
Some people might have found this situation interesting.
I just wanted to call the police right away.
Of course, nobody talked about the horse team again.
Tom and Miss Baker went back into the library.
Several feet of twilight were between them.
They went as if to watch beside a real body.
I tried to look pleasantly interested and a little deaf.
I followed Daisy around the connecting verandas.
We went to the porch in front.
We sat side by side on a wicker settee.
It was very dark there.
Daisy had her face in her hands.
It was as though she felt how lovely it was.
After a while, her eyes moved out into the dark.
I saw that her feeling was strong and not calm.
I asked questions about her little girl.
I thought they might help her feel calm.
"We do not know each other very well, Nick."
She said this all at once.
"Even if we are family.
You did not come to my wedding."
"I was not back from the war."
"That is true."
She kept waiting for a moment.
"Well, I have had a very bad time, Nick.
Now I do not see much good in anything."
It was clear she had a reason for feeling so.
I kept waiting, but she said nothing more.
After a moment, I talked about her daughter again.
I did not sound very sure of myself.
"I suppose she can talk, and eat, and everything."
"Oh, yes."
She looked at me without really thinking about me.
"Listen, Nick, I will tell you what I said.
I said it when she was born.
Would you like to hear?"
"Very much."
"It will show you how I have come to feel.
It can show how I feel about things.
Well, she was less than an hour old.
Only God knows where Tom was.
"I woke up from the ether feeling completely abandoned.
I asked the nurse right away about the baby.
Was it a boy or a girl?
She told me it was a girl.
So I turned my head away and started crying.
“All right,” I said.
“I am glad it is a girl.
And I hope she will be a fool.
That is the best thing a girl can be here.
She can be a beautiful little fool.”
"You see, I think everything is terrible," she went on.
Her voice was very sure.
"Everybody thinks so, all the people who know the most.
And I know.
I have been all over the place.
I have seen everything and done everything."
Her eyes quickly moved around.
She looked ready to fight anyone who thought different things.
She looked rather like Tom.
She gave a strong laugh, looking down on others.
"I know the world, God, I know it so well!"
Her voice stopped, and stopped making me listen and believe.
At once, I felt her words were not really honest.
That made me feel bad.
The whole evening felt like a game to fool me.
Perhaps she wanted to make me share some feeling.
I kept waiting.
Soon she looked at me with a smirk.
I knew that look would come.
Her lovely look said she was in a secret society.
It was a distinguished society to which Tom belonged too.
Inside, the deep red room was full of light.
Tom and Miss Baker were sitting on one long seat.
He was at one end, and she at the other.
She read to him from the Saturday Evening Post.
She talked in a quiet voice with no change.
Her words ran together like a song making people calm.
The lamplight was bright on his boots.
It was dull on her autumn-leaf yellow hair.
As she turned a page, light ran along the paper.
Slender muscles moved a little in her arms.
When we came in, she put up one hand.
She kept us quiet for a moment.
"There will be more," she said.
She let the paper fall on the table.
"You can read it in our next paper."
Her knee moved as if she could not rest.
Then she stood up.
"Ten o’clock," she said.
She looked as if finding the time on the ceiling.
"Time for this good girl to go to bed."
"Jordan is going to play tomorrow," Daisy said.
"The big game is over at Westchester."
"Oh, you are Jordan Baker."
Now I knew why I had seen her face before.
I had seen it in many rotogravure pictures.
They were of the sporting life at Asheville.
Others were from Hot Springs and Palm Beach.
Her face looked pleasing, though she looked down on others.
I had heard a story about her too.
It was a bad story that said something against her.
But I could no longer remember it.
"Good night," she said in a quiet voice.
"Wake me at eight, will not you?"
"If you will get up."
"I will.
Good night, Mr. Carraway.
I will see you soon."
"Of course you will," Daisy said.
"In fact, I think I will plan a marriage.
Come over often, Nick.
Then I will find a way to throw you together.
"I could lock you both in linen closets by accident.
Or push you out to sea in a boat.
You know, all that sort of thing."
"Good night," Miss Baker called as she went up.
"I have not heard a word."
"She is a nice girl," Tom said after a moment.
"They should not let her run around the country so."
"Who should not?"
Daisy asked this in a cold voice.
"Her family."
"Her family is one woman about 1,000 years old.
That woman is a sister of one of her parents.
Also, Nick is going to look after her.
Are not you, Nick?
"She will spend lots of weekends here this summer.
I think being with a family will be very good."
Daisy and Tom looked at each other for a moment.
They said nothing.
"Is she from New York?"
I asked this quickly.
"She is from Louisville.
We were white girls together there.
Our beautiful white lives—"
"Did you have a private talk with Nick outside?"
Tom asked this all at once, in a strong voice.
"Did I?"
She looked at me.
"I cannot seem to remember.
But I think we talked about the Nordic people.
Yes, I am sure we did.
We started talking about it, and then, you know—"
"Do not believe everything you hear, Nick," he told me.
I said in an easy way that I heard nothing.
A few minutes later, I got up to go home.
They came to the door with me.
They were side by side in a happy light.
As I started my car, Daisy called out.
Her voice made it clear I must listen.
"Wait!
I forgot to ask you something important.
We heard you plan to marry a girl out West."
"That is right," Tom said in a kind way.
"We heard you have made a promise to marry her."
"That is a lie about me.
I am too poor."
"But we heard it," Daisy said again.
She was open and lovely again.
This was a surprise to me.
"We heard it from three people.
So it must be true."
Of course, I knew what they were talking about.
But I had made no promise to marry anyone.
People had already talked as if I would marry her.
That was one reason I had come East.
You cannot stop seeing an old friend because people talk.
But I would not let their talk make me marry.
It felt good that they were interested in me.
Being rich no longer made them seem far away.
But I felt rather sick and did not understand.
I felt that way as I went away.
I thought Daisy should run out with her child.
But she did not seem to plan anything like that.
Tom had a woman in New York.
That was less of a surprise than the book.
How had a book made him feel so bad?
Something made him try an old way of thinking.
He was no longer happy just being strong and proud.
His heart must have needed something else.
It was deep summer on the roadhouse roofs.
It was deep summer in front of wayside garages too.
New red petrol-pumps sat in pools of light.
I reached my place at West Egg.
I put my car under its shed.
Then I sat on an abandoned grass roller outside.
I sat there in the yard for a while.
The wind had gone, leaving a loud, bright night.
Wings were beating in the trees.
The frogs made a persistent organ sound.
It was as if the earth had full bellows.
They blew the frogs full of life.
A moving cat made a dark silhouette in the moonlight.
Its silhouette wavered as it moved.
I turned my head to watch it.
Then I saw I was not alone.
A man was 50 feet away.
He had come from the shadow of my neighbour’s mansion.
His hands were in his pockets.
He looked at the silver pepper of the stars.
He moved without hurry.
His feet were in a secure position on the lawn.
I thought it must be Mr. Gatsby himself.
He looked ready to determine his share of our heavens.
I decided to call to him.
Miss Baker had talked about him at dinner.
That was enough reason to start talking to him.
But I did not call to him.
Something sudden told me he was happy being alone.
He stretched out his arms toward the dark water.
He did it in a curious way.
Even far away, I could have sworn he was trembling.
Without thinking, I looked out to the sea.
I saw only one little green light far away.
It might have been the end of a dock.
When I looked for Gatsby again, he was gone.
I was alone again in the dark, without quiet.
